articles.title: Physical modelling string synthesis in real time
articles.excerpt: Physical modelling synthesis generates sound by simulating the actual physical mechanics of vibrating matter rather than playing static wavetables or filtering raw geometric waveforms. While tradition…
articles.body: Physical modelling synthesis generates sound by simulating the actual physical mechanics of vibrating matter rather than playing static wavetables or filtering raw geometric waveforms. While traditional subtractive synthesis uses mathematical approximations like saw and square waves, and sample libraries replay pre-recorded audio recordings of instruments, physical modelling calculates the physical wave propagation, boundary reflections, internal material damping, and structural resonance of acoustic objects in code. When you pluck, strike, or bow an acoustic string, its sonic timbre evolves dynamically across every note.
articles.author: naman

articles.title: Delaunay triangulation and Voronoi geometry in real time
articles.excerpt: In computational geometry and procedural graphics, delaunay triangulation real time algorithms provide a method to generate clean, dynamic 3D meshes directly from shifting point clouds. While static m…
articles.body: In computational geometry and procedural graphics, delaunay triangulation real time algorithms provide a method to generate clean, dynamic 3D meshes directly from shifting point clouds. While static meshes rely on pre-baked vertex index buffers that remain rigid during performance, dynamic triangulation reconstructs the topological connectivity between vertices on every frame. When combined with its mathematical dual, the Voronoi diagram, artists can transform particle clouds, audio waveforms, and spatial simulations into fluid geometric surfaces, faceted crystalline shells, and organic cellular tessellations. In real-time audiovisual environments like Infinite , dynamic triangulation links sound synthesis with procedural 3D form.

articles.title: How YouTube Handles a Billion Hours of Video
articles.excerpt: Every day, people watch more than a billion hours of video on YouTube. That number is hard to picture, so here is a smaller one: more than 500 hours of video are uploaded every minute. The system has…
articles.body: Every day, people watch more than a billion hours of video on YouTube. That number is hard to picture, so here is a smaller one: more than 500 hours of video are uploaded every minute. The system has to accept that flood, convert every upload into a dozen playable formats, store it forever, and deliver it instantly to a phone on a slow connection in one country and a television on fiber in another, all while deciding which video to recommend next. The interesting part is not any single piece of that. It is how the pieces fit together so that no one part becomes a bottleneck that takes the rest down with it. Start with the upload, because everything downstream depends on a decision made in the first seconds.
articles.author: Mubashir Taj

articles.title: Why P2P WebRTC failed at 5 users, and how I built an SFU video + chat app with LiveKit, Laravel Reverb, and Next.js [Open Source]
articles.excerpt: Hey everyone! I'm a 20-year-old self-taught developer from Thailand preparing to break into the industry as a junior full-stack/backend dev. I recently built an open-source group video conferencing an…
articles.body: Hey everyone! I'm a 20-year-old self-taught developer from Thailand preparing to break into the industry as a junior full-stack/backend dev. I recently built an open-source group video conferencing and real-time chat app called Chatn. When I started, I thought I could just follow a basic WebRTC tutorial. But as soon as I tried scaling beyond 2 users on localhost, things broke down fast. Here are the main technical hurdles I ran into and how I solved them: The P2P WebRTC Bottleneck (Switching to LiveKit SFU) My first prototype used a standard WebRTC P2P mesh. It worked fine between 2 browser tabs. But with 4–5 participants, my laptop fan went crazy and video froze. In P2P mesh, connections scale as O(N²).

articles.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
articles.excerpt: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.
articles.body: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called dwarf galaxies , are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the most common type of galaxy in the whole universe.
